extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, mathematics enthusiasts, and readers interested in the aesthetics and practice of mathematical proof
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the value of alternative proofs of known theorems, emphasizing aesthetic, technical, and practical criteria beyond mere correctness. Focus is on what makes a reproof interesting, useful, or influential in mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revealing hidden connections
rubrics_metrics.description: Working backward from difficult theorems to simple results can reveal connections between different areas of math.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the proof exposes links between previously separate topics or techniques, e.g., deriving a difficult result by tracing it to elementary facts that highlight relationships across subfields. Consider whether the proof suggests new lines of inquiry by showing conceptual overlap rather than merely reproducing known steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative development
rubrics_metrics.description: "Somebody taking what they've done in the past and using that to create a technique and create a way to develop ideas" — proofs that embody creative technique development rather than mechanical problem-solving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the proof introduces or refines methods that can be reused or adapted, demonstrating the author's creative trajectory. Prefer proofs that encapsulate a technique or viewpoint that can seed further research, rather than proofs that are narrowly tailored tricks with no transferable insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bridging to deeper work (gateway proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: New proofs serve as gateways: "One day you're just looking at primes, and the next day you are looking at densities of squares."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the proof opens new conceptual territory or connects the theorem to broader themes, acting as a stepping stone to more advanced results. A strong gateway proof invites exploration beyond the original statement and suggests new problems or generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amusing complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: "The only way you want to do something difficult is that it's amusing." — the idea that difficulty should serve insight or intellectual pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer proofs whose complexity is justified by insight, surprise, or aesthetic enjoyment rather than gratuitous technicality. Penalize proofs that are convoluted without yielding clearer understanding; reward ones where cleverness illuminates rather than obscures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sparse elegance
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs demonstrating exceptional economy and clarity — an appreciation for concise, clear, and economical arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate succinctness and clarity: does the proof strip away unnecessary machinery and present the heart of the argument transparently? Favor minimal presentations that make the core idea visible and avoid bloated or opaque derivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical relevance / illuminating applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternative proofs may illuminate practical applications — e.g. potential connections between infinitude-of-primes results and cryptographic security — suggesting deeper relationships across domains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the proof suggests or clarifies applications outside pure theory, or points to implementations, heuristics, or connections with applied fields. Value proofs that make previously hidden practical consequences plausible or that translate abstract facts into usable insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newness / new perspective distinct from correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof can be "good" not for being the first of its kind but for offering a new perspective: economy, transferable technique, or surprising bridge. "Newness" is itself a value axis distinct from correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a reproof, treat novelty of viewpoint as a substantive criterion separate from correctness. Ask whether the proof provides a genuinely different conceptual framing, supplies a reusable method, or yields unexpected connections — even if it doesn't produce a stronger theorem.
